references.text: Matthew's parallel account of the raising of Jairus' daughter, where Jesus says the girl is not dead but sleeping, and the crowd laughed at him.
Mark's parallel account where Jesus comes to Jairus' house and finds people weeping and wailing, and says that the child is not dead but sleeping.
Jesus says that Lazarus has fallen asleep, but that he will wake him. Here sleep is used as a metaphor for death, just as in Luke 8:52.
Stephen 'fell asleep' when he died – the same imagery where death is described as sleep, as Jesus describes Jairus' daughter.
Paul uses the expression 'those who have fallen asleep' to refer to deceased believers, reflecting Jesus' description of death as sleep.
Paul writes that 'we will not all fall asleep' – again using sleep as a metaphor for death, consistent with Jesus' wording in Luke 8:52.
Abraham wept and mourned over Sarah when she died. Weeping and mourning over the dead is a recurring practice in the Bible, also seen in Luke 8:52.
The prophet Jeremiah mentions professional mourners who were called to lament over the dead, reflecting the same mourning practice we see in Luke 8:52.
Jesus says 'Do not weep' to the widow of Nain before raising her son – the same command as in Luke 8:52 where Jesus says 'Do not weep' before raising Jairus' daughter.
Elisha raises the Shunammite woman's son from the dead – an Old Testament parallel to Jesus' raising of Jairus' daughter.
Daniel refers to the dead as 'sleeping in the dust of the earth' and says they will wake up – death is described as sleep, just as Jesus does in Luke 8:52.
